t: 3654. Minimum Sum After Divisible Sum Deletions — Editorial
o:
## Understanding the problem
Repeatedly delete any contiguous subarray whose sum is divisible by k; elements are positive, so deletions never hurt and we want to delete as much total weight as possible. Example 2 deletes [1,4,1] (sum 6) then [3] (sum 3), leaving 5.

DP over prefixes keyed by prefix-sum remainder: dp[i] = minimum remaining sum for prefix i. Either keep element i (dp[i−1] + a[i]) or delete a block (j, i] whose sum ≡ 0 (mod k), landing on dp[j]. Blocks with the same remainder class are exactly prefixes sharing that remainder, so keeping the minimum dp per remainder in a hash map gives O(n).
k: A deletable block (j, i] exists iff prefix sums P[j] ≡ P[i] (mod k).
dp[i] = min(dp[i-1] + a[i], min{ dp[j] : P[j] ≡ P[i] (mod k), j < i }).
A hash map from remainder to minimum dp value makes each step O(1); positivity of elements guarantees deletions only reduce the sum.

a.i: Sweep left to right maintaining best[r] = minimum dp among processed prefixes with prefix-sum remainder r (seeded with dp[0] = 0 at remainder 0). At each element, dp = min(extend-without-deletion, close-a-deletion-block via best[current remainder]). Insert the new dp into the map afterwards.
s: For each x: pref += x; r = pref % k; dp = min(dp + x, best.get(r, ∞)).
a.t: O(n) — one pass with O(1) hash-map operations per element.
a.sp: O(min(n, k)) for the remainder map.

w: The remainder-bucket DP is optimal and elegant; an O(nk) table DP also works but wastes memory/time. Pitfalls: negative numbers would break the 'deletion always helps' assumption (constraints exclude them), forgetting the seed best[0] = 0 (needed to delete a prefix block), and modulo of negatives in JS. Follow-up: maximize deletions when elements can be negative, or count minimum number of deletion operations.
